newsitem.title: USA: Stocks, bonds rally after inflation report; dollar.
newsitem.headline: Stocks, bonds rally after inflation report; dollar.

text.p: Stocks and bonds rallied Friday for the first time this week after the government reported that producer prices rose only modestly last month, calming inflation jitters on Wall Street.
Corn and soybean prices fell to their lowest level in more than nine months after the government raised its estimate of this year's crop to near-record levels.
The dollar rallied and oil ended higher.
The Dow Jones industrial average rose 47.71 points to 5,969.38, bouncing back from four consecutive sessions of losses. For the week, the Dow fell 23.48.
In the broader market, advancing issues beat declines 1,433 to 864 on moderate volume of 395 million shares on the New York Stock Exchange.
The rally came on the sixth anniversary of the bull market, which started on Oct. 11, 1990.
The Dow index cracked the 6,000 level briefly on Monday and Tuesday, but finished lower both days.
Wall Street cheered news that the Producer Price Index rose a modest 0.2 percent in September, slightly less than expected, in a sign that inflation remained tame at the wholesale level.
In another report, retail sales increased 0.7 percent last month, above forecasts, but the report included a downward revision of August sales to a 0.2 percent decline.

"It has been a very powerful market," said Hugh Johnson, chief investment officer at First Albany Corp. "We were hitting on all cylinders and what launched it was the combination of good retail sales and a good wholesale inflation number."

In the inflation-sensitive bond market, the bellwether 30-year Treasury rose half a point, and the yield, which moves in the opposite direction from the price, fell to 6.85 percent from 6.89 percent on Thursday.
In currency markets, the dollar fell overnight in Tokyo but revived after Japanese buyers came to the rescue. It ended at 111.65 Japanese yen, up from Thursday's close of 111.28.
The dollar marched higher to close at 1.5305 German marks, compared with 1.5283 at Thursday's close.
In commodity markets, corn and soybean prices tumbled after the government raised forecasts for this year's corn and soybean crops.

The Agriculture Department raised its estimates for the corn crop to 9.01 billion bushels, which would be the third largest on record, from a previous estimate of 8.80 billion bushels. It raised its soybean estimate to 2.35 billion bushels -- the second largest crop ever -- from 2.27 billion.
"There's nothing friendly about the corn or bean numbers," said Don Roose, president of U.S. Commodities.

Corn for December delivery fell 6-1/4 cents to $2.83-3/4 a bushel at the Chicago Board of Trade, the lowest since December 1995. November soybeans fell the daily 30-cent limit to $7.00-1/4 a bushel, the lowest since January.

Cotton and orange juice prices also tumbled after the crop report. The November frozen concentrated orange juice contract fell 0.95 cent to 111.25 cents a pound at the New York Cotton Exchange. December cotton fell 2.20 cents to 73.20 cents a pound at the exchange.
Crude oil for November delivery rose 40 cents to $24.66 a barrel at the New York Mercantile Exchange.
Overseas, London's FTSE 100 index jumped 33.4 points to 4,028.1, and stocks in Tokyo also rose, with the 225-share Nikkei average up 97.33 points to 20,968.16.
